lesson.menu_desc: Asking a supplier abroad for better terms without damaging the relationship: diplomatic language that sounds firm and polite at the same time -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- The Supplier Call
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Plácido Perez Filho | Lesson 5 -- The Supplier Call
lesson.grammar_point: diplomatic language: I was wondering if you could, would it be possible to, might / could, it seems that, I'm afraid

listenings.text: One mistake I see a lot, especially with people who negotiate in a second language, is that they are too direct. They say: give me a discount, or: that's too expensive. In their language it might sound normal. In English it often sounds rude, and they don't even know it. The good news is that soft language doesn't make you weak. Saying I was wondering if you could lower the price asks for exactly the same thing. It just leaves space for the other side to say yes. And you can still say no. Of course you can. Just put I'm afraid in front of it, and give a reason. I'm afraid that's a deal-breaker for us, because our clients won't accept it.

Hello, this is David Lin from the sales team. I'm calling about your email from Monday. I'm afraid we can't lower the price by eight percent. With the cost of energy this year, it's simply not possible for us. But I'd like to make a counteroffer. If you could increase the order from forty to sixty tons, we could give you a three percent discount, and we could lock in the price until March. I think that's a fair way to meet halfway. Also, it seems that the down payment was a sticking point last time, so we could accept twenty-five percent instead of thirty. I'll follow up with the new quote by email this afternoon. Thank you.

A few years ago I was negotiating with a supplier in Malaysia, and we were stuck. We wanted ninety-day payment terms, and for them, that was a deal-breaker. They needed the money faster. So we had two weeks of emails, and nobody moved. What changed it? Leverage. I got a quote from another supplier, and I mentioned it, very politely. I said: I was wondering if we could find a solution, because we do have another option. Suddenly they were ready to talk. In the end we met halfway: sixty days, and a small discount if we paid earlier. Everybody was happy. And the lesson for me was: push back, but always leave the door open.
